title: Marbled murrelet habitat suitability in redwood timberlands of Northern Coastal California utilizing LiDAR-derived individual tree metrics
place: Humboldt and Del Norte Counties, northern coastal California, 238,355 ha of mostly second-growth redwood and Douglas-fir timberland; laser scan flown December 2017 to February 2018, occupancy surveys 1992 to 2021 (pp. 2, 6, 17)
response: 48 patches with occupied behaviour from audio-visual surveys, radar and direct evidence, 0.1 to 463.4 ha; 1,080 used points inside them against 117,804 available points from a balanced acceptance sample; not nests, only 1 of 26 California nest trees on private land in the study area (pp. 5, 6, 17)
predictors: airborne laser scanning, Riegl VQ-1560i at more than 40 pulses per square metre; 80 covariates on a 5 m grid from individual treetops, area-based canopy and percentile metrics, climate and geography (pp. 6, 7)
lidar_measures: density of treetops 60 m or taller in a 2 ha circle, positive and linear to 25 trees per ha; summed height of treetops 50 m or taller, positive to a plateau near 13,000 m; standard deviation of height of treetops 50 m or taller, positive to a peak at 10 m then falling; area-based canopy and percentile metrics weak (pp. 1, 12)
method: MaxEnt used-available model, four-phase covariate selection by AIC over 10 bootstrap resamples, regularization multiplier 2.0, 5 m grid with 2 ha moving windows (pp. 8, 12)
evaluation: AUC 0.99, average training AUC 0.989 (SD 0.001) over 10 replicates with random 80 to 20 per cent splits of used points; sensitivity 0.89, positive predictive value 0.49, Cohen's kappa 0.63 at threshold 0.19 on training data; no spatial hold-out (pp. 8, 14, 15, 21)
transfer: no
clayoquot_lidar_model: no, study area wholly in Humboldt and Del Norte Counties, California (p. 2)

id: a fine scale lidar based habitat suitability mapping methodology for the marbled murrelet brachyramphus marmoratus on vancouver island british columbia
title: A fine-scale lidar-based habitat suitability mapping methodology for the marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus) on Vancouver Island, British Columbia
place: Three sites on northern Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Holberg 155.12 km2, Koprino 87.53 km2 and Jeune Landing 405.62 km2, together 648.27 km2 and 0 to 12.57 km inland (p. 28); laser scans flown August to October 2012 (p. 31), aerial survey waypoints from 2005 and 2006 (p. 37), re-survey of 54 waypoints on 25 and 26 October 2015 (p. 43)
response: No nests or occupancy data at the sites (p. 7). Habitat suitability ranks 1 to 5 given by helicopter observers at 787 waypoints after cleaning (p. 37), copied to the 6197 lidar-detected trees taller than the median within 20 m of each waypoint, 99 of them Rank 1 and 67% Rank 4 (pp. 54, 74, 109). Re-survey matched 48% of original ranks and 85% of suitable or unsuitable classes (p. 72)
predictors: Airborne laser scanning acquired from Western Forest Products Inc., Optech 3100EA, mean 16.96 points per m2 (pp. 31, 33), giving 10 of 12 predictors by the thesis's count (p. 127); distance to saltwater from a provincial coastline and biogeoclimatic subzone from the provincial map (pp. 61, 62, 65)
lidar_measures: Linked to aerial survey suitability ranks, not to nests. Higher ranks with higher canopy rugosity above 10 m, dominant and co-dominant canopy heights of 30 to 70 m, trees 25 to 80 m tall, and canopy closure near 60% or above 80% (p. 114); from the lidar ground model, higher ranks with elevation below 600 m, slope 0 to 50 degrees, topographic ruggedness below 5 m and aspect 250 to 325 degrees (p. 113); local Moran's I class of tree height showed no clear link (p. 115). Terrain measures outranked every canopy measure in importance (p. 83)
method: Balanced random forest, R randomForest, 795 trees, each bootstrap draw capped at 495 trees to down-sample the commoner ranks (p. 69); 12 predictors on a 20 m grid or per tree, predicting ranks for about 2.5 million lidar-detected trees (pp. 54, 56, 65)
evaluation: Out-of-bag samples only, no independent or spatial hold-out and no field check of predictions (pp. 67, 129). Overall accuracy 71.05%, Kappa 0.51, class accuracy Rank 1 90%, Rank 2 86%, Rank 3 74%, Rank 4 67%, Rank 5 98% (p. 80); the Discussion misprints 71.95% (p. 108). Tree ranks averaged per survey polygon matched the existing polygon rank in 64.68% of polygons (p. 101)
transfer: No. The three sites were pooled in one model and no model was applied outside them (pp. 66, 67, 129)
clayoquot_lidar_model: No. Built on northern Vancouver Island from aerial survey ranks with no nest data (pp. 7, 28); Clayoquot Sound appears only in the background review (pp. 18, 23)

title: Modeling habitat for Marbled Murrelets on the Siuslaw National Forest, Oregon, using lidar data
place: Siuslaw National Forest, central Oregon Coast Ranges, with the model transferred from the neighbouring Coos Bay BLM District in Conservation Zone 3; surveys 1990s, lidar 2005 to 2014 (pp. 3, 5)
response: stand occupancy from Pacific Seabird Group intensive surveys, 772 stands, 553 occupied and 219 unoccupied (p. 5)
predictors: airborne lidar metrics from FUSION at 22.9 m summarised per base vegetation polygon, plus distance to the coast (p. 5, Table 1 p. 8)
lidar_measures: maximum canopy height positive in both transferred and local models; local model canopy relief ratio positive, skewness of return heights positive, variation in returns between 9.87 and 36 m negative; distance to coast negative (p. 9, Table 6 p. 11)
method: logistic regression at stand level; Coos Bay model with original coefficients, refitted to Siuslaw data, and a new model chosen by AIC from nine candidates (pp. 6 to 7)
evaluation: AUC, classification measures at threshold 0.716 and leave-one-out cross-validation; AUC 0.73 transferred, 0.79 refitted, 0.78 local (Table 3, p. 10); Table 3 does not say whether full-data or cross-validated
transfer: yes, Coos Bay model applied to Siuslaw National Forest, AUC 0.73 with original coefficients and 0.79 refitted, against 0.78 for the local model (p. 1, Table 3 p. 10)
clayoquot_lidar_model: no; Oregon survey stands and Oregon lidar only (pp. 3, 5)

title: Modeling marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus) habitat using LiDAR‐derived canopy data
place: Coos Bay BLM District and Elliott State Forest, Coast Range of southwestern Oregon; surveys 1993 to 2010 and 1992 to 2012, lidar 2008 (pp. 238 to 240)
response: stand occupancy from Pacific Seabird Group surveys, 121 occupied and 302 unoccupied Coos Bay stands, 130 occupied and 510 unoccupied Elliott State Forest stands for validation, and 11 nest trees (p. 239)
predictors: airborne lidar metrics from FUSION at 22.9 m summarised per stand, plus distance to the coast, compared with Gradient Nearest Neighbor imputed vegetation variables (pp. 240 to 241)
lidar_measures: maximum cover above mean height, maximum 99th and 10th percentile heights and SD of first-return cover above modal height larger in occupied stands; minimum kurtosis of height distribution smaller (pp. 242, 244); at nest trees maximum canopy height and cover above modal height larger (p. 244)
method: logistic regression with stepwise selection at stand level; use-availability logistic regression for nest trees on 3 by 3 blocks of 22.9 m pixels (pp. 240 to 241)
evaluation: AUC 0.74 and Cohen's kappa 0.24, leave-one-out accuracy 64, sensitivity 63, specificity 65 per cent; Gradient Nearest Neighbor model AUC 0.64, kappa 0.12; nest trees average AUC 0.91 (pp. 237, 242, 244)
transfer: yes, to the Elliott State Forest in the same study area, kappa 0.18, accuracy 51, sensitivity 91, specificity 41 per cent, no AUC reported (p. 244)
clayoquot_lidar_model: no; Oregon only (pp. 238 to 240)

title: Modeling Marbled Murrelet nesting habitat: a quantitative approach using airborne laser scanning data in British Columbia, Canada
place: Desolation Sound (training) and Clayoquot Sound (transfer test), south coast of British Columbia; nests radio-tracked 1998 to 2002, scans 2015 to 2019 in Desolation Sound and LidarBC 2020 in Clayoquot Sound (pp. 3 to 4)
response: presence-only nest locations from radio-tracked birds, 58 in Desolation Sound and 21 in Clayoquot Sound after 6 cliff nests were dropped from 85 under scan coverage, positional error about 50 m (p. 4)
predictors: airborne laser scanning (forest height, canopy surface area, forest vertical complexity, internal forest gaps) plus climate moisture index and distance to the coast (Table 1, p. 4)
lidar_measures: forest vertical complexity, the standard deviation of point heights in 1 ha, positive; internal forest gaps, the volume of empty 1 m3 voxels below and among the canopy in 1 ha, negative (p. 6); forest height and forest vertical complexity higher at nests than random forest in both areas (pp. 6, 9)
method: MaxEnt, regularisation 0.2, linear and product features, 10,000 background points, average of 20 bootstrap replicates, also ensembles of small models; 100 m grain (pp. 4 to 6)
evaluation: AUC and continuous Boyce index; internal bootstrap in Desolation Sound (70 per cent split, 100 runs) AUC 0.77 (SD 0.03), Boyce 0.99; good model AUC above 0.7 and Boyce above 0.5 (pp. 1, 5 to 6, Table 2 p. 8)
transfer: yes, trained in Desolation Sound and projected to Clayoquot Sound, AUC 0.63 and Boyce 0.67; top model chosen on scores from both areas (pp. 1, 5 to 6, Table 2 p. 8)
clayoquot_lidar_model: no; every model was trained in Desolation Sound and the 21 Clayoquot Sound nests and 2020 LidarBC scans were used only as a test set (pp. 3, 5)

title: Patch Scale Nest-Site Selection by Marbled Murrelets ( Brachyramphus marmoratus )
place: Clayoquot Sound, west coast of Vancouver Island, nests 2000 to 2002, and Desolation Sound, southern British Columbia mainland, nests 1999 to 2001; random plots sampled mainly in 2001 (Clayoquot) and 2004 (Desolation) (PDF pp. 3, 5)
response: radio-tracked nests reached on the ground against random old-growth plots; models used 142 sites, Clayoquot Sound 27 nests and 43 random, Desolation Sound 37 nests and 35 random; 8 of 36 Clayoquot and 76 of 121 Desolation nests unreachable; abstract says 64 nests and 82 random plots, Results give 78 random (PDF pp. 1, 3, 9)
predictors: field plots of 25 m or 75 m radius measuring canopy tree diameter, canopy height, canopy complexity as standard deviation of height, and platform tree density (Clayoquot only), with slope from a 25 m digital elevation model, ground-measured elevation and aspect (PDF pp. 4, 5, 6)
lidar_measures: none; field-measured canopy height and canopy complexity carried significant regional interactions (PDF p. 9), Clayoquot nests shorter (33.4 against 37.6 m) and less complex (4.9 against 6.0 m) than random, Desolation nests taller and more complex (PDF p. 10); complexity only a weakly negative trend in Clayoquot and not significant in its model (PDF pp. 10, 15)
method: logistic regression resource selection functions at the patch scale of 0.2 to 2.0 ha, models ranked by AICc or QAICc, region-specific and combined model sets (PDF pp. 1, 6, 7)
evaluation: resubstitution on the same data, no independent nests; best Clayoquot model Nagelkerke R squared 0.55 with 44 per cent of nests above 0.8, best Desolation model R squared 0.36 with 27 per cent above 0.8; region-specific models put 59 (Clayoquot) and 64 (Desolation) per cent of nests above 0.7 (PDF pp. 8, 9, 13)
transfer: no; a Desolation to Clayoquot test was considered and declined, and a pooled model without regional terms scored only 15 per cent of Clayoquot and 27 per cent of Desolation nests above 0.7 (PDF pp. 11, 13)
clayoquot_lidar_model: no, ground plots only and no transfer test (PDF p. 11)

id: habitat suitability mapping for marbled murrelets in clayoquot sound
title: Habitat Suitability Mapping for Marbled Murrelets in Clayoquot Sound
place: Ursus Valley, Clayoquot Sound, west Vancouver Island, field plots in 1998 with 22 of 93 plots from earlier years; model mapped over all of Clayoquot Sound, 335,127 ha on 36 map sheets (pp. 101, 102, 105, 113)
response: no nests; two principal component factors from 93 vegetation plots in 31 polygons, the first carrying epiphyte cover and the mean and variance of tree height (62.6 per cent), the second carrying platform density (18.6 per cent) (pp. 105, 110)
predictors: Vegetation Resource Inventory maps drawn by aerial photo interpretation (tree height corrected for elevation, stand age, basal area, vertical complexity, crown closure) and TRIM contour maps (distance from ocean, elevation) (pp. 103, 107, 115)
lidar_measures: none; the photo-interpreted analogues were mapped tree height, age and basal area, all positive, vertical complexity positive for the first factor [slope 1.47, p < 0.001] but with almost all polygons in one class, and crown closure scored best between 30 and 70 per cent (pp. 110, 112, 115)
method: Habitat Suitability Index from seven suitability curves set by 90th quantile least absolute deviation regression and the literature, combined as a geometric and arithmetic mean, at the grain of the inventory polygon (1.2 to 188 ha) and binned into Excellent, Good, Sub-optimal and Unsuitable (pp. 103, 106, 108, 112)
evaluation: none against nests; map variables checked against plots, tree height r = 0.858 and basal area r = 0.768 (p < 0.01, n = 93), and verification named as the next step (pp. 109, 116)
transfer: no transfer to another region; built in the Ursus Valley and applied untested to all of Clayoquot Sound, with adjustment said to be needed before use in other regions (pp. 113, 116)
clayoquot_lidar_model: no; a Clayoquot model from photo-interpreted inventory maps and vegetation plots, with no laser scans, no nests and no comparison with a transferred model (pp. 101, 107, 116)

id: estimating nest densities for marbled murrelets in three habitat suitability categories in the ursus valley clayoquot sound
title: Estimating Nest Densities for Marbled Murrelets in Three Habitat Suitability Categories in the Ursus Valley, Clayoquot Sound
place: Ursus Valley, Clayoquot Sound, west Vancouver Island, 1998, 1999 and 2000 (pp. 121, 123)
response: 5 nests (1 active, 4 from earlier years) found by climbing 467 trees with potential platforms around 44 random plots, 240 trees in Excellent, 139 in Good and 88 in Sub-optimal habitat, all nests in Excellent (pp. 121, 128)
predictors: classes of the Bahn and Newsom index from photo-interpreted Vegetation Resource Inventory maps, with field plot measures of tree height, height variance, diameter, epiphytes, canopy closure and platforms (pp. 123, 125, 127, 131)
lidar_measures: none; field-measured mean tree height (25 ± 6 m against 15 ± 2 and 13 ± 4 m) and variance of tree height (180 ± 102 against 57 ± 16 and 43 ± 23) were higher in the Excellent class where all nests lay, though that class was also 630 m or more lower (p. 127)
method: stratified cluster sampling by tree climbing, one-way analysis of variance, nest density from a random effects Monte Carlo model with Taylor expansion, at the grain of the 15 m plot and climbing cluster within inventory polygons (pp. 125, 126)
evaluation: nest density 0.53 ± 0.24 visible nests per ha (95 per cent confidence interval 0.05 to 1.0) and 0.11 ± 0.12 active nests per ha per year in Excellent, 0 in Good and Sub-optimal, with a 6 and 20 per cent chance of finding no nest had density matched Excellent; no discrimination score (pp. 128, 129)
transfer: no; tested in the valley where the index was built, with tests elsewhere on Vancouver Island, the mainland and the range recommended (p. 134)
clayoquot_lidar_model: no; tested a photo-interpreted inventory model with 5 climbed nests, no laser scans and no transferred model for comparison (pp. 121, 123, 131)
